title: Pre-Debit Notification: What It Is and How to Respond
metaDescription: A pre-debit notification warns you at least 24 hours before a recurring debit. Learn what it says, how to pause, opt out or cancel, and why alerts get missed.
h1: What is a pre-debit notification, and how should you respond to one?
summary: A pre-debit notification is an advance alert, sent at least 24 hours before a recurring debit, that gives the merchant, amount, date and mandate reference for that charge. Under the RBI's 2026 e-mandate directions, the issuer must send it for covered card and UPI mandates, and you can opt out of a single debit or of the whole mandate. If you do nothing, the debit goes ahead on the scheduled date unless it needs an authentication step you have not completed.
stepsHeading: How to respond to a pre-debit notification

steps.name: Read the notice before the due date
steps.text: Open the alert and check the merchant name, the amount, the date and time of the debit, and the e-mandate reference. Compare them with the subscription you signed up for. A mismatch is a reason to act, not just to wait.

steps.name: Decide what you want
steps.text: You can let the debit go through, opt out of this one debit, pause the mandate for a period, or cancel it. These are different actions, so read the options before you tap anything.

steps.name: Act in the app or portal that holds the mandate
steps.text: In Google Pay, tap the notification to see the details, then pause or cancel the mandate with your UPI PIN. For a card mandate, sign in to the issuer's mandate portal, such as HSBC's MandateHQ, and pause or cancel with the OTP sent to your registered mobile number.

steps.name: Confirm the status changed
steps.text: In Google Pay, open Autopay and check the Live tab to see whether the mandate now shows as paused or cancelled. On a bank portal, keep any reference number it gives you. A request on screen is not proof of cancellation until the status changes.

steps.name: Cancel the service with the merchant too
steps.text: Stopping a mandate stops future debits, but it may not end your account with the merchant. Cancel the subscription itself, and check your next statement for any debit that still goes through.

sections.heading: What the notice has to say
paragraphs: The RBI's 2026 directions set the minimum content for a pre-transaction notification. It must tell you the merchant's name, the transaction amount, the date and time of debit, the reference number of the e-mandate, and the reason for the debit, which is that you registered an e-mandate. The issuer must also let you choose the channel, such as SMS or email, and let you change it later.

The notice is not the debit. It is a warning sent before any money moves, and it is the point where you can still opt out. Once the debit has been processed, the matter moves to the post-transaction alert and to your issuer's grievance process.

sections.heading: When the notice arrives
paragraphs: The directions require the notice at least 24 hours before the actual charge. Google Pay's help page says you get a notification 24 hours before any debit from the bank. Its help pages also say the notice does not appear for automatic top-ups on FASTag or NCMC metro and transit cards, which the RBI exempts as well.

Some debits need more than a notice. HSBC's e-mandate FAQ describes a notice asking you to authorise a debit above a set amount, and says you cannot approve it after the scheduled debit date. That FAQ still uses a ₹5,000 threshold, which is older than the ₹15,000 limit in the current RBI directions, so check the amount rule against the directions rather than the FAQ.

sections.heading: Why notices get missed
paragraphs: A notice can only reach you through the channel you picked. If your phone number or email on file is out of date, the alert may never arrive. The RBI directions let you change the channel, so check which one is active in your bank or card settings.

App alerts can be switched off in your phone's notification settings, and an SMS can be missed after a number change. If you think you missed one, check the mandate's status in the Live or Pending list of your UPI app, or in your card issuer's portal, before the due date.

sections.heading: What pausing and cancelling change
paragraphs: Pausing and cancelling are not the same. Google Pay lets you pause a live mandate with a start and end date you choose. HSBC's MandateHQ lets a paused mandate be resumed, but a cancelled mandate cannot be reactivated and has to be registered again.

A cancelled mandate is final, so only cancel when you are sure you want the service to stop. If you are unsure, a pause buys time to check the merchant's terms, your account and your next statement without losing the mandate.

sections.heading: Keeping track in Essara
paragraphs: Pre-debit notices arrive one at a time, in different apps, so it is easy to miss the ones that matter. Essara's UPI AutoPay tracker lets you add each mandate and subscription yourself and shows upcoming auto-debits for the week and month, so you can see what is due before the notice does. Essara does not read your bank's alerts, your SMS or your UPI app, so the list is only as current as the entries you make.

faqs.q: Do I have to respond to a pre-debit notification?
faqs.a: No. If you do nothing, the debit goes ahead on the scheduled date, unless it needs an authentication step that you have not completed. Respond only if you want to skip, pause or cancel the debit.

faqs.q: Can I skip one payment without cancelling the whole mandate?
faqs.a: The RBI directions require the issuer to let you opt out of a particular transaction or of the whole e-mandate. Whether your app lets you skip one debit, or only pause for a date range, depends on the app, so read the options in the notice.

faqs.q: Are FASTag and metro card top-ups covered by the notice?
faqs.a: No. The RBI exempts FASTag and NCMC auto-replenishment mandates from the pre-transaction notice, because those top-ups recur without a fixed schedule. Google Pay's help page notes the same exception.

faqs.q: What should I do if a debit happened without any notice?
faqs.a: Raise it with your issuer in writing and keep the reference number. The RBI directions require issuers to run a grievance redressal system, and the RBI's customer liability rules apply to recurring e-mandate transactions.

faqs.q: Does a pre-debit notice mean the money has already left my account?
faqs.a: No. The notice is sent before the debit, so it confirms what is scheduled, not what has been paid. Post-transaction alerts are the ones that confirm a debit has happened.
